summary: American consumers are increasingly unwilling to pay high prices for new cars, leading to changes in buying behavior such as downsizing, purchasing used vehicles, and seeking better deals. Dealership traffic has slowed, with more buyers opting for less expensive models.
key_points: Consumers are reaching their limits on what they will pay for new cars.
Buyers are shifting toward downsizing and used vehicles.
Longer car loans and deal-hunting are becoming more common.
Dealership owners report slower traffic and increased demand for cheaper cars like the Chevrolet Trax.
Financial strain is evident as some buyers live paycheck to paycheck and carry debt.
source_name: American Consumers Have Had It With High Car Prices - WSJ
raw_snippet: Those days are coming to an end. Increasingly stretched consumers are starting to draw the line on what they will pay for a new car, according to dealers, analysts and industry data. Car buyers are downsizing, buying used vehicles, taking on longer car loans and holding out for deals. “People are asking, ‘How can I afford this?’” said Robert Peltier, who owns dealerships in East Texas. He said traffic, while still solid, has slowed at his dealerships and more customers are gravitating toward less-costly cars such as the pint-size Chevrolet Trax. “There are people who are in debt and living paycheck to paycheck.”

summary: The DeepSeek-R1-Zero approach applies reinforcement learning similar to RLHF but skips the supervised fine-tuning stage, calling it "pure" RL. Instead of human preference-based rewards, it uses accuracy rewards verified by automated systems and format rewards assessed by an LLM judge.

Reinforcement learning in LLMs here differs significantly from traditional RL.

raw_snippet: Still, this RL process is similar to the commonly used RLHF approach, which is typically applied to preference-tune LLMs. (I covered RLHF in more detail in my article, LLM Training: RLHF and Its Alternatives.) However, as mentioned above, the key difference in DeepSeek-R1-Zero is that they skipped the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage for instruction tuning. This is why they refer to it as "pure" RL. (Although, RL in the context of LLMs differs significantly from traditional RL, which is a topic for another time.) 尽管如此，这个强化学习过程与常用的 RLHF 方法类似，后者通常用于对 LLMs 进行偏好微调。（我在文章《LLM Training: RLHF and Its Alternatives》中更详细地介绍了 RLHF。）然而，如上所述，DeepSeek-R1-Zero 的关键区别在于他们跳过了用于指令调优的监督微调（SFT）阶段。这就是他们称之为“纯”强化学习的原因。（尽管在 LLMs 的语境下，强化学习与传统强化学习有很大不同，这又是另一个话题。）  For rewards, instead of using a reward model trained on human preferences, they employed two types of rewards: an accuracy reward and a format reward. 对于奖励，他们没有使用基于人类偏好的奖励模型，而是采用了两种类型的奖励：准确性奖励和格式奖励。  The accuracy reward uses the LeetCode compiler to verify coding answers and a deterministic system to evaluate mathematical responses. 准确性奖励使用 LeetCode 编译器来验证编程答案，并使用一个确定性系统来评估数学回答。  The format reward relies on an LLM judge to ensure responses follow the expected format, such as placing reasoning steps inside <think> tags. 格式奖励依赖于 LLM 裁判来确保回应遵循预期格式，例如将推理步骤置于 <think> 标签内。

raw_snippet: 经销商甩货：茅台失去控价能力 与所有白酒企业一样，茅台采取了 “经销商 + 自营” 的销售体系，尤其各地庞大的经销商群体更是链接各地优质客户资源的桥梁，是茅台创造既往辉煌的一大功臣。 不过在现实运营中，经销商体系也暴露出种种弊端。 如腐败（历任茅台高管腐败均与此密不可分），又比如茅台集团失去对终端价格的控制力（53 度飞天茅台 1499 的指导价在零售市场形同虚设），又比如在茅台旺季之时，各地经销商会囤积居奇，不仅可以赚得更大 “价差”，且茅台酒越发具有的金融属性也为经销商提供更为便利的融资条件，严重影响的社会影响。 尽管问题重重，茅台集团层面（尤其李保芳在任时）曾加大对自营渠道建的设（在电商平台开店，开发 i 茅台自营平台），不过最终也并未根本上颠覆经销商体系，2025 年前三个季度茅台经销商较上年末增加了 205 家。

summary: 茅台集团通过控制飞天茅台供应保持高价，但系列酒市场化程度高且利润低，导致经销商因成本压力不得不低价甩卖系列酒和放量飞天，反映出供需管理失控的局面。
key_points: 加盟商体系和配货支持是系列酒取得成绩的重要优势，自营渠道难以代替。
飞天茅台作为稀缺资源通过限制供应维持高价，系列酒则在竞争激烈的中低端市场且需求受大环境影响较大。
2023年飞天茅台批发价涨至1169元/瓶，实际成本考虑其他费用恐超过1500元/瓶。
经销商为了维护现金流，先低价甩卖系列酒，再因无效放量甩飞天茅台。
抖音封停低价茅台显示经销商放量飞天茅台，反映出作为供需调节管理的失控局面。
raw_snippet: 如今复盘彼时对加盟商体系的治理更多是 “多内” 管理，若没有加盟商 “配货” 的支持，系列酒很难有今日之成绩，这是自营渠道所不具备的优势。  对经销商来说，就有了以下两种经营思维：  非完全市场化的飞天茅台，作为接近奢侈品的稀缺性资源，茅台集团可以通过控制供应令其市场售价维持在较高水平，以往屡试不爽；  完全市场化的系列酒，系列酒在我国中低端白酒中可谓是联强环伺，且其需求最易受大环境波动影响（受众也是价格敏感型），产品很难有太大利润，但为了拿到配额的飞天，只能被动拿货。  2023 年茅台将一批价涨至 1169 元/瓶，彼时大环境尚未完全恢复，其涨价逻辑也并非主流媒体所倾向的 “市场导向”，而是管理层自认为有信心能够通过对供需关系的调节，让经销商保有足够的利润，并能同步给系列酒带量。  如今再来看，这恰是茅台需要反思的，飞天和系列酒一批价的上涨直接加重了经销商的成本，有媒体测算虽然 53 度飞天的批发价为 1169 元，但若算上各类成本以及系列酒的 “倒贴”，每瓶飞天的成本恐不低于 1500 元。  当大环境影响市场信心，经销商为维护其现金流：低价甩卖系列酒——无效后系列酒增速放缓——保现金流甩飞天。  说回此次抖音封停低价茅台，背后所反应的并非是简单的 “用茅台引流”，而是经销商已经开始放量飞天，茅台集团引以为傲的对供需关系的管理已经失控，其本质乃是：充分市场化的系列酒出货难，利润差，为缓解压力只能放量飞天。

raw_snippet: 1）传统流通渠道：高成本+低效率。以商超、杂货店为代表的传统流通渠道是国内最早的渠道形态，覆盖了大量下沉市场，是国内线下零售网络的基石，目前占比仍在60%以上。  但一方面流通渠道层级冗长，层层加价，叠加各种进场费、条码费等入场费用，导致品牌方成本居高不下，利润被中间环节蚕食，最终转嫁到消费者身上，产品价格虚高。  另一方面，由于货品经过多级的仓储和流转才会到达货架，周转率低下导致零食的新鲜度普遍不高，对于品牌方来说，也会面临账期长、无法快速响应市场变化等问题导致效率低下。  2）零食品牌专营店：高成本+高效率。 21世纪初，以来伊份为代表的零食品牌专营店横空出世，第一次将零食从散装、非标品提升到品牌化的高度。另外，相较于传统流通环节冗长的渠道层级，零食品牌专营店砍掉了经销商，采用短链经营（工厂——品牌中心仓——品牌门店），并建立了高标准的门店系统，提升了商品的新鲜度和购买体验，对物流、仓储等各个环节的信息流也实现了完全的自主掌控，效率大幅提升。 但弊端在于为了打造品牌形象，零食品牌专营店普遍开在核心商圈等黄金地段，导致门店的运营成本高，最终带来的结果就是产品高溢价，客流量和复购率低，坪效很难提升。

summary: Meta通过将数据中心产权置于第三方并对残值提供担保，实质上等同于向Blue Owl获得约280亿的债务融资，隐含票面利率约10.7%；但通过权利义务与会计处理的错位，该安排将现金流和会计利润压力推迟并弱化（会计上确认为经营租赁）。
key_points: 数据中心产权不属于Meta，273亿票据的发行人也非Meta，但Meta对剩余价值提供残值担保，若提前终止需补足差价（初始约280亿）。
实质上等同Meta向Blue Owl发出一笔规模约280亿的公司债，按前四年每年约30亿的租金计算，隐含票面利率30/280≈10.7%。

会计处理被设定为经营租赁而非融资租赁，从而降低当期会计利润压力；按GAAP，融资租赁会在前期确认更高的折旧与利息费用。

raw_snippet: 1）Meta视角：高融资成本=表外负债+短期现金流压力小  从表面看，数据中心的产权并不属于Meta，且273亿的票据发行人也不是Meta。  但Meta作为租户，在这笔交易中做了残值担保——数据中心的前16年运营期内，Meta如果提前中止租赁，那么需要补足数据中心剩余价值与约定值（初始为280亿）的差价。  因此上述操作看似兜了一圈，实则等效于：  在前16年内，Meta面向Blue Owl发了一笔规模280亿的公司债用于投入建设数据中心，每期支付利息相当于每年的租金，比如按前四年的租赁合同，就是每年约30亿，隐含票面利率30/280=10.7%。  虽然这个票面利率看上去很高，远高于Meta半个月前的公司债利率水平。但Meta用牺牲未来现金流换来的是：  1）权利义务周期错位：当期可以立即拿钱开工，但第一笔31亿利息在四年后2029年才开始支付，前四年的票据利息由Blue Owl来承担。  2）降低当期会计利润压力：尽管从实际责任划分上看，Meta才是数据中心的主导运营方。但通过硬性做义务不等的股权划分以及不做Meta收回产权的设定，使得这在会计确认上，仍然属于是一笔经营租赁而非融资租赁。  虽然融资租赁同样能减轻当期现金流压力，但在GAAP美国会计法下，融资租赁对当期利息支出确认（包含折旧费用+利息费用），前期往往会显著高于实际支付的租金。

raw_snippet:
二、盈利效率下坡路：压制估值的真正病因

除了现金流，从上述经营租赁还是融资租赁的差异点可以看出，Meta同样担心AI投入对利润的影响。海豚君认为，这恰恰是压制Meta 2026年估值表现的关键！

1、折旧成本压力是累积性的

截至到三季度，Meta的资本开支已经占到了当期收入的38%，拉高速度非常快。粗粗算下来，如果未来三年资本开支投入比例（实际很可能更高，而高峰期投入强度会达到收入的50%，假设这部分主要为服务器投入，那么按照Meta目前平均5.5年的服务器折旧周期来算，也意味着这笔投入在后续每年对利润率的压力就有7pct之多！（=38%/5.5，加入收入无法有效摊销折旧金额）。

哪怕是存在对旧设备的替换，与之前不到收入20%的投入规模相比，也要至少额外多承担3pct的利润率影响。但实际上，替换的旧服务器单价值远远抵不上源源不断的新投入，Meta的“Property and equipment”账面价值四年来一直水涨船高。

summary: The text explains the economics of cloud service providers, breaking down how 100 yuan of revenue is allocated among costs, operations, and profit, and emphasizing that cloud services are essentially capital‑intensive infrastructure businesses. It highlights that most costs lie in hardware and data center build‑out, while software and interconnects are relatively small but crucial, and shows via a chart that high‑performance compute (GPU) can deliver a high return on investment over four years.
key_points: Cloud service providers operate like capital‑intensive infrastructure businesses, similar to power plants or walls of capital.
A sample economic breakdown for cloud providers: out of 100 yuan of revenue, 55 yuan is cost, 10 yuan is operating expenses, and 35 yuan is profit.
Hardware and physical infrastructure (servers, GPUs, machines, cabling, cooling, etc.) constitute the bulk of costs; software and interconnects are smaller but essential components.
Cloud services integrate hardware, software, and capital into a unified product that is monetized through cloud access and SaaS offerings.
A key principle is to keep costs low while maximizing utilization of expensive GPUs, which can be used for many years if well managed.

The English chart titled "The High ROI of High Compute Performance" shows that a 4‑year AI infrastructure costing about $1B (including DC facility, GPU compute, and networking) can generate a 4‑year rental opportunity of about $2.5B at $4 per GPU‑hour.
Within that 4‑year rental opportunity, increased utilization (15%) is valued at roughly $350M and a 25% performance increase is valued at roughly $600M, illustrating the high ROI of powerful compute.
Source of the chart is cited as 英伟达NDR材料 (NVIDIA NDR materials).
raw_snippet:
1.1）从云服务商的经济账说起：到底谁赚了红利，谁赚了吆喝，谁担了风险？

A. 云服务商们的经济账：100元收入分布——55元成本、10元运营开支、35元利润；

以下，海豚君用一产产业链一本简单的经济账来给大家仔细算下数，来直观了解一下这场三年的AI赛崛斗中。我们知道，云服务是一个既要资金壁垒，又重技术壁垒的行业。它的前半部分跟盖房子一样，需要把厂房盖起来、机柜、布线、冷却等都要做好，这部分需要巨额的资本投入。

软装部分就是放入GPU、CPU，这中间GPU内部的连接、GPU与GPU，以及与其他设备的连接要做好，再加上网络、宽带、通电上电，软装基本完成。这些要素要放在一起，再通过技术人员完成功能、形象端统一、整合一化为基础的IaaS服务了。

从上述的要素其实可以看出，虽然它听起来高大上，本质上没有摆脱宽带电信的老路——把各种重资产+技术组合在一起，形成云服务，通过通道租给云服务终端。

这个生意的核心就是，成本要足够低，比如说成本最高的GPU装上去了之后可以用个十年八载的，不能像光伏电场那样，隔三差五光伏板就要更换掉。

summary: The expert highlights Shopify's evolution from serving small businesses to aggressively targeting the enterprise segment with Shopify Plus, emphasizing ease of use and a robust ecosystem as key reasons behind customer choice.
key_points: Shopify has shifted from focusing solely on small businesses to targeting larger enterprises.
The Shopify Plus offering is designed for enterprise and medium business clients, distinct from the core product.
Key differentiators include cost, low barrier to entry, simplicity, and a strong ecosystem of partners and apps.
raw_snippet:
I believe what was very apparent in the ecosystem as soon as even probably five years was that there was always a big platform choice for merchants of all sizes. Merchants had choices between things like Adobe Commerce or Magento as it was known, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, WooCommerce, which is WordPress's e-commerce ecosystem. There has been a really, really large shift towards brands of all sizes moving towards Shopify.

...there has been this large shift towards focusing on being enterprise-ready, highlighting some of the larger brands that they're working with, really promoting their Shopify Plus product.

It's really important to note the clear distinction between Shopify and Shopify Plus. Shopify Plus is very much angled towards enterprise and medium business and above, whereas the Shopify entry product is very much all organized and built in a way where it's built for that mom-and-pop shop or the person who's starting out in e-commerce.

summary: Shopify's growth in the B2B space is constrained mainly by limitations in platform functionality for complex B2B requirements, but investments and improvements are ongoing.
key_points: Shopify's adoption in B2B is limited due to functional gaps for layered pricing, SKU visibility, and complexity.
Shopify is investing heavily to address B2B gaps and become a more serious player in the space.
Prioritization of enterprise needs may resolve current hesitation among B2B brands.
raw_snippet:
Yes, I do. I do believe some brands in the B2B space are hesitant to move to Shopify. I believe that they feel that Shopify may not be completely ready for B2B, but I do know that that is an area that Shopify is investing into heavily and is developing a lot further to be able to cater to more of that market.

Typically, when you have a B2B platform where you're selling to various different stakeholders, you will have different layers of pricing, different layers of SKUs that are available to be seen by different B2B merchants. That just requires a lot of development and a lot of feature building that simply takes quite a lot of time.

If you're already running a very successful business like Shopify is and you're winning a lot on the direct-to-consumer B2C space, it's a matter of prioritizing which budgets are allocated where. It's just a time thing, but where they're heading with that, they will be a very, very serious player.

summary: Lean, agile product teams and targeted sales strategies are fundamental to Shopify's rapid enterprise growth, setting it apart from larger, less nimble competitors.
key_points: Shopify forms lean, effective product teams to develop enterprise features quickly.
The company employs highly targeted sales teams for specific enterprise niches.
Public promotion and leadership messaging are key to winning large brands.
raw_snippet:
I think it's having very, very, very good, lean, agile product teams that are able to execute on building out features and making products enterprise-worthy. I also think they've done incredibly well at building sales teams that are very targeted at very specific niches and verticals within that enterprise space.

I do think they've done incredibly well in terms of the way that they promote themselves publicly, whether it be from senior leadership or advertising, to really encourage those larger brands to consider Shopify.

summary: Shopify's ease of use and vast app ecosystem allow brands to avoid specialist coding staff, making it cost-effective and scalable relative to competitors like Salesforce and Adobe.
key_points: Shopify enables plug-and-play functionality via its extensive app ecosystem.
Running a Shopify site typically requires less specialized internal engineering support than incumbent platforms.
Cost, ease of integration, and streamlined maintenance are viewed as major advantages by brands.
raw_snippet: I think the ease of use and the ease of connecting everything together. Typically, brands that for example, if they had a Salesforce Enterprise website just as an example, and this is very similar with Adobe and historically Magento, you really need a very dedicated expert engineer almost to be working for you on a full-time basis internally to be able to support that website. Whereas with Shopify, there's so many ready-to-go plug-and-play apps that cover so much of that functionality and so much readily available SaaS within the Shopify ecosystem that it can be serviced at a much less costly manner than what has typically been available in the past.

summary: Shopify leads in ecosystem and community development, but its growth is mainly limited by areas it cannot serve due to payment restrictions and by the need to improve partner management.
key_points: Shopify has built a robust ecosystem of agency and tech partners, surpassing competitors.
Its share of global e-commerce platforms is around 15%, with ambitions to reach 30% or more.
Shopify cannot serve some large sectors due to Stripe payment restrictions (e.g., firearms sales).
raw_snippet:
Shopify now accounts for close to 15% of all e-commerce globally platform-wise. I see no reason why that wouldn't be heading towards closer to 30% by this time next year so double.

Shopify currently, because of that relationship they have on the payment side of things with Stripe, they do not work in some what's considered restricted industries.

For example, they don't currently work with large outdoors brands as an example, or outdoor e-commerce stores. ... because they sell firearms and ammunition, Shopify don't work with them. I see that as an area where the incumbents are very heavily invested and winning is in the areas that are currently restricted by Shopify and Stripe's payment restrictions.

summary: Despite price increases, brands tend to remain with Shopify due to the ecosystem's cost-saving opportunities, even amidst some pushback around platform fee hikes.
key_points: Shopify and its ecosystem partners (like Klaviyo) have raised prices, leading to some pushback.
Brands still see the value in the aggregate savings and efficiency gains of the Shopify ecosystem.
Opportunity and total cost of ownership outweigh the downsides of platform or app fee increases.
raw_snippet: I think no one's ever happy when prices go up. That's very relative to this industry in general. I know that companies like Klaviyo, for example, recently did the same thing and they had pushback. I know that Shopify has had pushback when they've raised prices in the past. I think the thing that brands do tend to remember though, is that the sheer amount of opportunity and areas to save money by being in that Shopify ecosystem still outweighs the fees and the price hikes.

summary: Shopify’s ecosystem success is driven by its decision to focus on core platform features while relying on extensive third-party partnerships for complementary services, a strategy actively doubled-down as it moves upstream.
key_points: Shopify decided early not to build all functionalities itself—instead fostering a thriving partner ecosystem.
Key partners provide major services (subscriptions, shipping, loyalty, reviews, etc.).
As Shopify targets larger/enterprise clients, it increases partnership depth with bigger agencies and tech vendors.
raw_snippet:
They've always been heavily focused on that ecosystem. I think that was really smart of them to say, "Hey, we're going to build the best e-commerce platform. The easiest to get started, the easiest to get up and running, but we are not going to build subscriptions, shipping information, foreign currency calculators, app conversion tools, loyalty, reviews, wishlists."

...as they continue to move upmarket and swim upstream more and more into enterprise, more and more into B2B, they've realized that that is one of their true core strengths.

They've continued to double down on partnerships, albeit in a slightly different capacity because now they're moving towards larger agencies...

summary: Shopify's partner enablement is hampered by limited staffing and over-reliance on lean teams, resulting in some existing partnerships receiving less attention than necessary.
key_points: Shopify partner managers are overextended and struggle to maintain equal relationships with all partners.
More staff and diverse personalities are needed to personalize and strengthen agency relationships.
Agencies have significant influence and can shift to competitive platforms if not adequately supported.
raw_snippet: Yes. I think personally they are understaffed to be able to service all of their partners. I think they end up with some partners, and I know this from getting a lot of first-hand conversations with agency partners as well as my peers on the tech side, they all seem to be working with too many partners. I think that's an area where whilst it is good that they stay lean and be smart in all of those sorts of things, the gap is that they just simply don't have enough team members to properly manage those partnerships. I think sometimes they are focusing more on new partnerships than existing partnerships.

summary: Internal planning and organization within brands are the biggest bottlenecks in Shopify onboarding and scaling, more so than Shopify-specific technical difficulties.
key_points: A lack of clear internal timelines and planning reduces onboarding and platform migration efficiency.
Many delays stem from organizations rather than inherent Shopify challenges.
Organizational readiness is the most common hurdle in platform adoption.
raw_snippet: I think some of the frustrations that I hear that the internal teams don't necessarily have strong plans or time frames or timelines on integration and that therefore the timeline of swapping platforms or starting on a new platform if they're a smaller business takes longer than they originally planned for or thought. I would say it's probably lack of planning and organization would be the biggest hurdle that brands face when they come on board with Shopify, and it's very common.

summary: Shopify Plus merchants benefit from priority, personalized support, which is a core selling point and supports Shopify's move into enterprise and upmarket segments.
key_points: Shopify Plus offers rapid, higher-touch support including real-time calls, not just chat or tickets.
A dedicated team sells the upgrade to Shopify Plus based on enhanced service levels.
Personalized service is crucial for enterprise clients and retention.
raw_snippet: Shopify Plus, the customer service side of things is very, very effective. They pride themselves on being able to be there to support customers very quickly should in the rare occasion they need support arise. The reason for that is that's one of the big things that they sell. There's a whole team that sells brands to just move from Shopify to Shopify Plus, and it's quite a large team. That's a big part of what is part of the selling point is that you get priority support.

summary: Shopify’s omnichannel POS and payment infrastructure create defensible advantages, enabling connected commerce across online and offline sales with a single centralized system.
key_points: Shopify's POS product enables unified payments and omnichannel commerce with no direct peer among competitors.
Its open-loop system allows seamless transactions online and offline within a centralized payment ecosystem.
This infrastructure builds a competitive moat, especially attractive to omnichannel enterprises.
raw_snippet:
Very much so. Case in point is that POS product. There's not really anyone else who's doing that. Salesforce doesn't have the ability to do that, Adobe doesn't have the ability to do that. It's not even a closed-loop ecosystem, it's really an open-loop ecosystem because they're giving the merchant the opportunity for their customers to be able to check out anywhere, whether it be online or in person, and that all ties into their one centralized payment system.

They really are pioneering this "connected commerce", "omnichannel experience" and unified commerce. That is a big part of what they're doing.

summary: Shopify’s payment and POS advancement is hindered by exclusion from restricted verticals due to Stripe partnership limitations; addressing this would open significant new markets.
key_points: Transaction fees via Stripe are a common frustration among merchants, seen as relatively high.
Shopify's payment policies currently exclude industries like firearms, impacting growth in those verticals.
Changing these restrictions could quickly expand Shopify’s enterprise market share.
raw_snippet:
I think the transaction fees, which are managed essentially through a partnership with Stripe, can be high. I think that's where merchants can get a little frustrated is they're paying high percentages on their transaction fees.

as I mentioned earlier, they're not servicing a lot of these so-called restricted verticals...but because of Stripe's policies on the payment side, they don't want to service that industry. That to me is something that they should change immediately because it opens up such a large market for them who would want to work with them, who have said that they would work with them.

summary: Emerging competition such as Shopware may threaten Shopify’s momentum if not closely monitored, echoing past market shifts when incumbents failed to adapt.
key_points: Shopware is identified as potentially agency- and developer-friendly with growing buzz in the Shopify ecosystem.
Shopify risks becoming complacent and missing new rivals if they emulate old incumbents.
Adaptability and vigilance are necessary to avoid market stagnation.
raw_snippet:
I think there are some upcoming platforms that they may not be paying attention to that they probably could. A good example of one, and I don't know a lot about this platform, it is relatively new, but I do hear a lot of agencies that are part of the Shopify ecosystem looking at this platform, and that's Shopware.

I think a blind spot could be that they become like the incumbent platforms and don't pay attention to the up-and-comer and evolve to match or to suit because that happens with a lot of businesses and it's happened with their incumbents where they were too slow moving, too big to adapt and adjust to what the market wanted, which is what Shopify has became now.

summary: The expert views AI-native entrants such as OpenAI and Anthropic as meaningful threats, especially if they shift from partnerships to direct transaction capability, potentially bypassing Shopify’s value proposition.
key_points: AI-driven tools (e.g., ChatGPT) are rapidly shifting user behavior and could reduce reliance on Shopify-hosted stores.
If customers transact entirely within AI interfaces, Shopify’s merchant value could diminish.
The current partnership between Shopify and OpenAI is beneficial, but future competition is possible.
raw_snippet:
I'll be interested to see if ChatGPT and OpenAI themselves don't build a more transactable e-commerce environment, they obviously have a partnership with Shopify. For how long that partnership is, we don't know. They could be using that to learn and gather and plan to do things themselves. That I would see as a potential blind spot and potential threat because ChatGPT and OpenAI are building a lot of different suites and products. They just recently came out with their own Internet browser.

If ChatGPT had that functionality available for the whole of the Internet, then I think it makes the Shopify product less valuable because someone doesn't even have to go to the Shopify website to even transact with a brand. Instead, it's being done in this microeconomy of AI and ChatGPT.

summary: Loyalty programs, one-click checkout, and reduced friction in purchasing are now standard consumer expectations, influencing brand and platform choice.
key_points: Consumers demand loyalty incentives and seamless checkout experiences.
Shopify invests in features like one-click Shop Pay to reduce checkout friction.
Brands must implement loyalty and streamlined checkout processes to stay competitive.
raw_snippet:
Loyalty is definitely growing a lot more and more when typically brands want to be more involved with their customers and customers want to be more involved with their brand. Loyalty is a big part of that. Consumers expect to be rewarded for their loyalty. They want discounts from loyalty points, they want discounts at checkout for redeeming loyalty points so that's a big part of it. Checkout, the quicker someone can check out, the easier...Shopify actually released them around how quick people expect to be able to check out and transact on a website.

Removing that friction is super important for brands to focus on, and it's obviously a big part of what Shopify has done with being able to use one-click Shop Pay at checkout if you are a part of Shop Pay or using Shop Pay.

summary: The expert emphasizes the significance of tech partners' market health (such as Klaviyo) as an indicator of Shopify's continued growth, with strong mutual integrations driving new brand conversions.
key_points: Klaviyo and other partners are tightly integrated in the Shopify ecosystem and growing rapidly.
The success of these partners suggests future Shopify growth due to symbiotic relationships.
Brands using high-growth partners are likely to migrate toward Shopify.
raw_snippet:
I think one thing that's really important is paying attention to the other growing SaaS that's happening in this environment. You have a look at Klaviyo, they've gone up 30% on the stock market within I think it's the last month. They're growing so much, they're very, very, very heavily integrated into the Shopify ecosystem. They're one of Shopify's largest tech or SaaS partnerships. They focus on email, SMS, all of those sort of things that help that customer journey, and they're very integral to Shopify's success. Paying attention to what's happening with partners like that, particularly Klaviyo, is really a good indicator of where Shopify is headed as well.

If the other publicly listed partners of Shopify are growing and doing well, you can bet your bottom dollar that Shopify is going to continue to grow and do well because brands that are on Klaviyo that might be on an incumbent platform will 100% be encouraged to switch to Shopify in the future.

summary: The expert describes a major industry shift over the past five years from a fragmented platform landscape toward Shopify, driven by technology upgrades and emerging AI/ML capabilities in e-commerce. Shopify is increasingly chosen across merchant sizes as AI agents and automation become central to future positioning.
key_points: Historically, merchants selected among multiple platforms like Adobe/Magento, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, and WooCommerce.
There has been a “really, really large shift” of brands of all sizes moving toward Shopify as their core platform.
Newer developments center on AI and machine learning, especially AI agents, with brands and platforms positioning themselves to exploit these technologies.
raw_snippet:
I believe what was very apparent in the ecosystem as soon as even probably five years was that there was always a big platform choice for merchants of all sizes. Merchants had choices between things like Adobe Commerce or Magento as it was known, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, WooCommerce, which is WordPress's e-commerce ecosystem. There has been a really, really large shift towards brands of all sizes moving towards Shopify.
I think that's probably been the largest shift that has happened in e-commerce in general. I think some of the newer kind of things that are shifting and changing are definitely towards AI and machine learning and how AI agents play a role in the future of e-commerce and seeing brands and platforms position themselves to take advantage of that in the best way possible.

summary: Shopify has evolved from serving small “mom-and-pop” merchants to supporting larger, more complex businesses via its app ecosystem, though B2B remains a work-in-progress. The expert believes resource‑intensive B2B functionality is still developing, causing some B2B brands to hesitate.
key_points: Shopify originally targeted small businesses doing roughly $1–5M in revenue and was not built for B2B or large SKU catalogs.
Competing platforms like Salesforce Commerce Cloud and Adobe Magento historically handled large SKU counts and B2B complexity better.
The growth of a powerful app ecosystem now allows Shopify to serve “brands of all shapes and sizes.”
Some B2B brands still feel Shopify is not fully ready, but Shopify is heavily investing to close this gap.
raw_snippet:
I think the update of technology. Shopify originally as an example was a really, really good platform that catered to businesses that did from $1 million-$5 million. They're really catered to the mom-and-pop entrepreneur who were looking to jump online and start their e-commerce journey. Typically, platforms like Shopify who were angled towards small business really couldn't handle B2B.
They really couldn't handle large amounts of SKUs that other platforms really were able to, such as Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Adobe Magento, etc. I think this ecosystem of Shopify is so powerful and there's so many apps that can be plugged into Shopify now. It really makes it a tool that is available for all brands of all shapes and sizes.
…
Yes, I do. I do believe some brands in the B2B space are hesitant to move to Shopify. I believe that they feel that Shopify may not be completely ready for B2B, but I do know that that is an area that Shopify is investing into heavily and is developing a lot further to be able to cater to more of that market.

summary: The expert explains why B2B e-commerce is harder for Shopify to fully support, emphasizing layered pricing, SKU visibility, and complex stakeholder structures. Building this functionality requires significant development resources and prioritization against Shopify’s strong D2C business.
key_points: B2B platforms must support multiple stakeholders with different pricing tiers and product visibility rules.
These layered requirements add complexity beyond typical D2C commerce and demand extensive feature development.
Shopify must decide how much budget and resources to allocate to B2B, given its existing D2C success.
The expert expects Shopify to become a serious B2B player once these investments mature, reducing B2B hesitation.
raw_snippet:
Typically, when you have a B2B platform where you're selling to various different stakeholders, you will have different layers of pricing, different layers of SKUs that are available to be seen by different B2B merchants. That just requires a lot of development and a lot of feature building that simply takes quite a lot of time.
If you're already running a very successful business like Shopify is and you're winning a lot on the direct-to-consumer B2C space, it's a matter of prioritizing which budgets are allocated where. It's just a time thing, but where they're heading with that, they will be a very, very serious player. I think it will remove a lot of hesitation for people looking to switch over from a B2B standpoint.

summary: Shopify’s organizational design—lean, agile product teams and tightly focused sales efforts—is highlighted as a key advantage over incumbents like Salesforce and Adobe. This structure enables rapid enterprise feature delivery and targeted vertical penetration.
key_points: Shopify avoids the boom‑and‑bust hiring cycles seen at Salesforce and others by building small, efficient product teams.
These teams are effective at both building and servicing products.
Shopify has created specialized sales teams targeting specific niches and verticals in the enterprise space.
Public promotion by leadership and advertising further accelerates enterprise adoption.
raw_snippet:
To be honest, I think they already have taken on board some of those lessons. I think they're very good at building lean, agile, and effective teams. Whereas I think from my experience of those other platforms, particularly companies and platforms like Salesforce, they often go through really large hiring sprees, but then they also go through really big firing sprees when they completed development of things or when things aren't going in the direction that they want to. I think Shopify has been very, very smart around building these individual product teams that are very lean and efficient at building products and servicing products.
…
Once again, I think it's having very, very, very good, lean, agile product teams that are able to execute on building out features and making products enterprise-worthy. I also think they've done incredibly well at building sales teams that are very targeted at very specific niches and verticals within that enterprise space. I do think they've done incredibly well in terms of the way that they promote themselves publicly, whether it be from senior leadership or advertising, to really encourage those larger brands to consider Shopify.

summary: Shopify has deliberately repositioned itself beyond small merchants by pushing Shopify Plus as an enterprise-focused offering, while maintaining its core SMB product. The speed of this shift and early wins with large brands impress the expert.
key_points: Messaging has shifted from purely “mom-and-pop” to emphasizing enterprise readiness and large-brand case studies.
Shopify Plus is clearly differentiated as the product for medium and enterprise businesses; the core Shopify remains aimed at small merchants.
Shopify has rapidly won major brands and met enterprise feature requests quickly.
The expert is “shocked” by the pace at which Shopify has become enterprise-capable.
raw_snippet:
I think Shopify have really focused their positioning on shifting away from just focusing on the messaging around the mom-and-pop and the early e-commerce person that's starting out on their journey. Whilst they do still focus on that, there has been this large shift towards focusing on being enterprise-ready, highlighting some of the larger brands that they're working with, really promoting their Shopify Plus product.
It's really important to note the clear distinction between Shopify and Shopify Plus. Shopify Plus is very much angled towards enterprise and medium business and above, whereas the Shopify entry product is very much all organized and built in a way where it's built for that mom-and-pop shop or the person who's starting out in e-commerce.
…
How quick they've done it. I think they've done it incredibly quick. I think they're starting to win brands and they've already won some very large brands behind the scene. They have done very, very well at making that shift quickly and being able to cater to those large brands' individual product feature requests very quickly. I think what shocked me is the speed at which that has progressed.

summary: The expert argues that Shopify’s usability and rich app marketplace lower operating costs for enterprises compared to legacy platforms that require dedicated in‑house engineers. This simplicity is a major driver of large-brand adoption.
key_points: Salesforce, Adobe, and Magento implementations often need full‑time expert engineers to support the site.
Shopify offers many ready‑to‑use “plug‑and‑play” apps and SaaS tools covering common enterprise needs.
As a result, merchants can run complex commerce stacks with less internal technical overhead and cost.
Ease of connecting tools within Shopify’s ecosystem is highly valued by larger brands.
raw_snippet: I think the ease of use and the ease of connecting everything together. Typically, brands that for example, if they had a Salesforce Enterprise website just as an example, and this is very similar with Adobe and historically Magento, you really need a very dedicated expert engineer almost to be working for you on a full-time basis internally to be able to support that website. Whereas with Shopify, there's so many ready-to-go plug-and-play apps that cover so much of that functionality and so much readily available SaaS within the Shopify ecosystem that it can be serviced at a much less costly manner than what has typically been available in the past.

summary: Shopify’s ecosystem strategy—deep agency and SaaS partner networks—is portrayed as its defining competitive moat and a challenge for incumbents to replicate. The expert believes the gap versus competitors like Adobe, Salesforce, and BigCommerce is now “too big.”
key_points: Shopify has aggressively built strategic agency partnerships across all merchant sizes to drive website builds and platform choice.
It has also cultivated a broad SaaS partner ecosystem for subscriptions, shipping, FX, tariffs, email, SMS, etc.
This combination yields a strong community and ecosystem that incumbents lack and may not have time or willingness to build.
To compete, incumbents would need to lower fees, improve product friendliness, and promote more effectively—changes the expert doubts they will execute.
raw_snippet:
I personally feel that the gap is too big now and the momentum that Shopify has gained is just too massive now. I do think that they really need to strip back their fees, make their product friendlier, promote their product better, focus more on building an ecosystem. One of the things that is quite unique to Shopify in a way is the way that they've built out their ecosystem. They've been very focused on building out strategic agency partnerships to build the websites for merchants of all sizes, whether it's small, big, medium, or in between.
They've also really focused on building this great ecosystem with SaaS partners who can service all of the things like subscriptions, shipping, foreign currency calculation, tariffs now, there's apps for that, email marketing, SMS, all of the other components that are needed for e-commerce to be successful. Shopify has built an outstanding ecosystem and community for that. I think the ability for a Salesforce or a Adobe or one of the other incumbents to be able to do that, I just don't think they have the time and maybe even the willingness to do that.

summary: The expert forecasts aggressive growth for Shopify’s global e-commerce share—from ~15% to a potential 30% within a year—and sees no clear ceiling given its ecosystem and agency dominance. Agency preferences are portrayed as a powerful long‑term demand driver.
key_points: Shopify is estimated to account for nearly 15% of global e-commerce platforms today.
The expert sees “no reason” this couldn’t reach ~30% within a year.
Websites are typically replatformed every 5–8 years, during which Shopify almost always enters the consideration set.
Shopify commands an estimated 60–70% share of agencies, which heavily influence merchants’ platform choices.
raw_snippet:
I believe Shopify now accounts for close to 15% of all e-commerce globally platform-wise. I see no reason why that wouldn't be heading towards closer to 30% by this time next year so double.
…
I don't really see a ceiling because they've been so smart about the way that they're listening to what the market wants, the way that they gather feedback from their ecosystem, the way that they incorporate that ecosystem. They're so far ahead of their competition in those elements. Where any brand is looking to replatform or redo their website, I would be very surprised if Shopify isn't a part of that conversation.
…
Even though they might only have, let's call it, 10%-15% of the current Internet e-commerce websites now, they definitely have closer to 60%-70% of all agencies now. A lot of what happens with e-commerce sites is that the agency of choice will drive the platform selection.

summary: Shopify’s focus on integrated payments and POS creates substantial growth optionality, especially in unified online–offline commerce, but high transaction fees and restricted verticals are weaknesses. Payment‑related policies tied to Stripe exclude lucrative segments like firearms/outdoor retail.
key_points: Shopify emphasizes payments and Shopify POS as major growth areas, enabling integration of online and offline sales.
Merchants sometimes perceive payment transaction fees (via Stripe) as high, generating frustration.
Stripe partnership rules prevent Shopify from serving “restricted” verticals such as retailers selling firearms and ammunition.
Incumbent platforms are strong in these restricted industries, representing a lost opportunity for Shopify unless policies change.
raw_snippet:
One thing to consider also too is Shopify has such a strong focus on payments. They've got a really big focus on their Shopify POS product, their point-of-sale product. They really focus on the fact that that can integrate with online and offline. That's a really big area for growth opportunity for them, but their payment rates can be a little high. I think that will be something that they need to adjust. The other component of that is that Shopify currently, because of that relationship they have on the payment side of things with Stripe, they do not work in some what's considered restricted industries.
For example, they don't currently work with large outdoors brands as an example, or outdoor e-commerce stores. We could use Academy Sports as an example. Really, really large e-commerce brand, but because they sell firearms and ammunition, Shopify don't work with them. I see that as an area where the incumbents are very heavily invested and winning is in the areas that are currently restricted by Shopify and Stripe's payment restrictions.

summary: Merchants react negatively to price hikes from Shopify and other SaaS vendors, but still perceive net value due to efficiencies gained within the Shopify ecosystem. Total cost of ownership, especially staffing and maintenance, remains a central consideration favoring Shopify.
key_points: Pricing increases by Shopify and peers like Klaviyo draw pushback from merchants.
Despite higher fees, brands often conclude that cost savings and opportunities within the Shopify ecosystem outweigh the price.
In TCO analysis, merchants compare SaaS plugin costs, platform fees, and transaction costs against staffing and maintenance requirements.
Shopify’s simpler, more streamlined system typically requires less internal technical staffing than incumbent platforms.
raw_snippet:
I think no one's ever happy when prices go up. That's very relative to this industry in general. I know that companies like Klaviyo, for example, recently did the same thing and they had pushback. I know that Shopify has had pushback when they've raised prices in the past. I think the thing that brands do tend to remember though, is that the sheer amount of opportunity and areas to save money by being in that Shopify ecosystem still outweighs the fees and the price hikes.
…
I would say they look at the costs of all of the SaaS plugins, they look at the cost of the platform and the monthly ongoing costs and the potential transaction costs, and then I think they weigh that with because it is a simpler, more streamlined system even with all of the plugins installed, it's much easier for them to then work with an external agency because the amount of upkeep and maintenance is very minimal. Whereas versus the incumbent platforms, they're often, as I mentioned earlier, having to hire a dedicated internal resource to consistently manage that website.
…
I would say staffing is a part of the decision when weighing up the costs, I would say it's one of the major considerations.

summary: Shopify’s partner ecosystem has been central to its success, but the expert believes partner management is under-resourced and uneven. As Shopify moves further upmarket, strengthening and better resourcing partner relationships—especially with agencies—becomes critical.
key_points: From the outset, Shopify chose to focus on core commerce and rely on partners for subscriptions, shipping, loyalty, etc.
The company has used tech and agency partners not only for co‑selling but also for deep product feedback and testing.
As Shopify moves into enterprise and B2B, it is “doubling down” on partnerships with larger agencies.
The expert sees a gap: partner teams are understaffed, overextended across too many partners, and sometimes prioritize new over existing relationships.
Human dynamics mean partner managers may favor “easier” agencies, risking neglected but important relationships.
raw_snippet:
They've always been heavily focused on that ecosystem. I think that was really smart of them to say, "Hey, we're going to build the best e-commerce platform. The easiest to get started, the easiest to get up and running, but we are not going to build subscriptions, shipping information, foreign currency calculators, app conversion tools, loyalty, reviews, wishlists."
…
The other thing that they've done really, really well is they've gotten the product very early on into the hands of very smart, creative individuals who build e-commerce websites. They've constantly taken that partnership not just as an opportunity to help co-sell, partner, and build business together, they've taken it as an opportunity to get really detailed, ingrained, proven product testing and feedback. I think that has just continued to serve them. I think what they've realized now is that as they continue to move upmarket and swim upstream more and more into enterprise, more and more into B2B, they've realized that that is one of their true core strengths.
…
Yes. I think personally they are understaffed to be able to service all of their partners. I think they end up with some partners, and I know this from getting a lot of first-hand conversations with agency partners as well as my peers on the tech side, they all seem to be working with too many partners. I think that's an area where whilst it is good that they stay lean and be smart in all of those sorts of things, the gap is that they just simply don't have enough team members to properly manage those partnerships. I think sometimes they are focusing more on new partnerships than existing partnerships.
…
What happens is if you have a human who is a partner manager and they get along with three agencies really well but they may not have the exact same partnership or strength of relationship with two agencies and they're supposed to be giving those five agencies all of their time equally, it's human nature that they're going to divert to the easiest three as opposed to spending time on the other two. I think that needs to change.

summary: Shopify Plus merchants receive much more personalized and responsive support, which is leveraged as a key selling point for upgrading. This premium support model underpins Shopify’s move upstream into enterprise accounts.
key_points: Shopify Plus customer service is described as “very, very effective” and highly prioritized.
A dedicated team promotes upgrades from Shopify to Shopify Plus, with priority support as a major benefit.
Plus merchants can receive support via phone or video calls rather than only ticket/chat channels.
Building this service capability has been intentional to support Shopify’s enterprise strategy.
raw_snippet:
Shopify Plus, the customer service side of things is very, very effective. They pride themselves on being able to be there to support customers very quickly should in the rare occasion they need support arise. The reason for that is that's one of the big things that they sell. There's a whole team that sells brands to just move from Shopify to Shopify Plus, and it's quite a large team. That's a big part of what is part of the selling point is that you get priority support.
Instead of having to lodge a ticket through a chat functionality, that support can sometimes be a phone call depending on the size of the Shopify Plus business or a Zoom call or a Google Meet call. It's a lot more personalized, it's a lot more one to one, it's a lot more dedicated. I think they've really focused on building that side of the business up to be able to support their shift upstream to more enterprise merchants.

summary: Shopify’s POS and payments infrastructure are portrayed as a unique, defensible “connected commerce” moat that rivals have not matched. The system allows merchants to unify online and in‑person checkouts through a single payment stack.
key_points: Shopify POS enables customers to check out anywhere—online or offline—feeding into one centralized payment system.
Competing platforms like Salesforce and Adobe lack comparable POS capabilities.
The expert frames Shopify as pioneering “connected commerce,” “omnichannel,” and unified commerce experiences.
Extending POS and unified payments to more enterprise brands will further strengthen Shopify’s competitive moat.
raw_snippet:
Very much so. Case in point is that POS product. There's not really anyone else who's doing that. Salesforce doesn't have the ability to do that, Adobe doesn't have the ability to do that. It's not even a closed-loop ecosystem, it's really an open-loop ecosystem because they're giving the merchant the opportunity for their customers to be able to check out anywhere, whether it be online or in person, and that all ties into their one centralized payment system.
They really are pioneering this "connected commerce", "omnichannel experience" and unified commerce. That is a big part of what they're doing. I think building on that and opening that up to more and more enterprise brands continues to build a big moat for them because no one else has even touched that side of things yet.

summary: The expert recommends that Shopify relax its restrictions on certain verticals imposed via Stripe and sees this as a quick, high‑impact win. Serving large, currently excluded merchants (e.g., firearms/outdoor chains) would expand Shopify’s POS and payments footprint significantly.
key_points: Many big omnichannel brands in restricted categories want to use Shopify but are blocked by Stripe’s policies.
These brands often have hundreds of stores and sizable online volume, representing substantial GMV.
Changing policy to support these verticals would open a “very easy quick win” market for Shopify.
This move would also bolster the company’s POS and payments growth strategy.
raw_snippet: Easy one that I can see as a huge win is that, as I mentioned earlier, they're not servicing a lot of these so-called restricted verticals. As I mentioned earlier, there's big enterprise brands that they could be working with that have hundreds of bricks-and-mortar stores, very big online sales, but because of Stripe's policies on the payment side, they don't want to service that industry. That to me is something that they should change immediately because it opens up such a large market for them who would want to work with them, who have said that they would work with them. I think that is a very easy quick win for Shopify is to change that policy.

summary: Emerging competitors like Shopware and AI‑driven players such as OpenAI/ChatGPT are flagged as strategic blind spots that could threaten Shopify’s trajectory if ignored. The expert warns Shopify not to become complacent like today’s incumbents.
key_points: Shopware is gaining buzz as a developer‑ and agency‑friendly platform building an ecosystem reminiscent of Shopify’s early playbook.
The expert fears Shopify might mirror incumbents by underestimating up‑and‑coming platforms and failing to adapt.
OpenAI/ChatGPT could build its own transactable e-commerce environment, potentially reducing the need for merchants to maintain Shopify storefronts.
If end‑to‑end checkout occurs inside ChatGPT for the entire internet, Shopify’s value proposition and fee structure could be questioned by merchants.
raw_snippet:
I think there are some upcoming platforms that they may not be paying attention to that they probably could. A good example of one, and I don't know a lot about this platform, it is relatively new, but I do hear a lot of agencies that are part of the Shopify ecosystem looking at this platform, and that's Shopware.
I think a blind spot could be that they become like the incumbent platforms and don't pay attention to the up-and-comer and evolve to match or to suit because that happens with a lot of businesses and it's happened with their incumbents where they were too slow moving, too big to adapt and adjust to what the market wanted, which is what Shopify has became now. Obviously, there's going to be up-and-comers that they need to be aware of and take notice of and shift and change so that they don't become like their previous incumbents if that makes sense.
…
I'll be interested to see if ChatGPT and OpenAI themselves don't build a more transactable e-commerce environment, they obviously have a partnership with Shopify. For how long that partnership is, we don't know. They could be using that to learn and gather and plan to do things themselves. That I would see as a potential blind spot and potential threat because ChatGPT and OpenAI are building a lot of different suites and products.
…
If ChatGPT had that functionality available for the whole of the Internet, then I think it makes the Shopify product less valuable because someone doesn't even have to go to the Shopify website to even transact with a brand. Instead, it's being done in this microeconomy of AI and ChatGPT. I think that's a threat because then merchants are looking at it like, "Well, why am I paying X amount of dollars to Shopify when people aren't even visiting my Shopify site to be able to transact?"

summary: The expert is skeptical that downmarket site builders like Wix and GoDaddy can threaten Shopify, despite their AI initiatives. Conversely, AI‑first platforms like OpenAI and Anthropic are viewed as potentially highly disruptive to e-commerce.
key_points: Wix is perceived as basic and is rarely considered by serious e-commerce agencies or experts.
The proliferation of “AI features” across SaaS is seen as noise; Shopify’s deep integration with leading AI (OpenAI) is differentiated.
AI‑first entrants could change consumer behavior by shifting time and transactions into AI environments rather than traditional web search.
This shift could gradually erode Google’s dominance and reshape how consumers discover and transact with brands online.
raw_snippet:
I just don't really think people take them seriously. I think Wix is still seen as, very basic in its functionality. It's never anything I hear spoken about by the experts in e-commerce who are putting out and building websites for brands day in and day out and doing very good at it. I think those brands are too far downstream to have any meaningful impact regardless of what AI is put into it. The other thing that happens with the AI thing is that it just becomes noise. Everyone, every SaaS, every e-comm, everyone's using AI. Once again, Shopify was really smart by doing that specifically with the most well-known AI and the most popular and utilized AI. It's just on a different level.
…

summary: Traditional SaaS metrics don’t fully apply to AI-native businesses because each additional customer incurs meaningful compute and inference costs that compress gross margins; rapid ARR growth can coexist with margins around 40–50% rather than the 80–90% typical in legacy SaaS. Founders should prioritize unit economics and compute efficiency over legacy benchmarks like Rule of 40.
key_points: In traditional SaaS, new users were near-zero marginal cost, but AI-native customers consume GPU cycles, electricity, and model inference time.
These non-zero marginal costs compress gross margins even as revenue grows quickly.
Some AI companies can scale to $50M ARR fast but show margin profiles closer to 40–50%, not 80–90%.
Software improvements are outpacing hardware, making it more expensive to run top models (Gorkem quote).
Founders should redefine "healthy growth" by focusing on unit economics that balance growth with compute efficiency rather than legacy benchmarks.

raw_snippet: 1. The old SaaS metrics don’t fit perfectly in the new AI economy. 1. 旧有的 SaaS 指标在新的 AI 经济中并不完全适用。 In traditional SaaS, every new user was almost pure profit. But for AI-native companies, each additional customer consumes GPU cycles, electricity, and model inference time. 在传统 SaaS 中，每一个新用户几乎都是纯利润。但对于以 AI 为本的公司，每增加一个客户都会消耗 GPU 周期、电力和模型推理时间。  These non-zero marginal costs compress gross margins, even as revenue growth skyrockets. Some AI companies are scaling from zero to $50 million ARR in record time—but with margin profiles closer to 40–50%, not 80–90%. 这些非零边际成本压缩了毛利率，即使收入增长迅猛。一些 AI 公司以创纪录的速度从零扩展到 5000 万美元 ARR——但毛利率更接近 40–50%，而不是 80–90%。  “Advancements in software are happening faster than advancements in hardware,” said Gorkem. “It’s getting more expensive to run the best models—even as we scale.” “软件的进步比硬件的进步更快，”Gorkem 说道。“即使我们在扩展，运行最优模型的成本也在变得更高。”  For founders, this means redefining what “healthy growth” looks like. Focus less on legacy benchmarks like Rule of 40 or gross margin expansion, and more on unit economics that balance growth with compute efficiency. 对于创始人来说，这意味着需要重新定义‘健康增长’的含义。少关注像 Rule of 40 或毛利率扩张这样的传统基准，更多关注在增长与计算效率之间取得平衡的单位经济学。

key_points: COGS (cost of goods sold), specifically compute cost, is the new primary constraint versus CAC in AI.
Founders cannot sustain both high COGS and high CAC, so products should be designed to "sell themselves" through product quality, virality, and community.
The model rewards teams that build sticky, habit-forming products and leverage organic distribution rather than outbound sales.

summary: The text explains why Palantir can sustain strong growth by using its unique FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) model, which differs from traditional project-based SaaS. Instead of building many custom versions, Palantir builds a highly configurable platform and sends engineers on-site to bridge the gap between generic product capabilities and specific customer needs, enabling both deep customization and scalability.
key_points: Palantir uses a business model centered on FDEs (Forward Deployed Engineers), who work on-site with clients to adapt the product to real-world use cases.
The FDE model originated from Palantir’s work with U.S. intelligence agencies, where direct understanding of user workflows was difficult, forcing iterative demos and feedback.
Palantir realized that instead of creating separate versions or heavy one-off customizations, it should build a highly customizable platform and let FDEs configure it per scenario.
Headquarters product and engineering teams focus on abstraction and generalization, turning early ‘gravel roads’ into ‘highways’ that can serve the next 5–10 customers.

This approach superficially resembles traditional project-based software development, which is often criticized for poor scalability, leading some to view Palantir as a consulting firm rather than a true software company.

Despite skepticism, Palantir’s market value has surged from under $15B at ChatGPT’s launch to around $500B, outpacing many oil majors and large banks, and it remains a major external SaaS provider to governments.
The article frames Palantir as an AI SaaS ‘new giant’ and uses its performance to explore how AI-driven SaaS can fundamentally change business logic and outcomes.
source_name: Article on Palantir and its FDE model (AI SaaS “new giant” case study)
raw_snippet:
为什么 Palantir 可以交付这样的增长？它和传统做项目制开发的 SaaS 公司有什么区别？

Palantir 的关键商业模式叫做 FDE，全称是 Forward Deployed Engineer（前线部署工程师）。意思是一位技术人员带着智能体驻扎在客户现场，填补产品功能与客户需求之间的差距。

这是硅谷创业者们最关心的一个问题。前 Palantir 高管（也是第二位工程师）Bob McGrew（同时也是前 OpenAI 首席研究官）在一档播客中表示，过去一年他参加的所有会议里，本以为创始人们会找他聊 ChatGPT，但结果是，所有人都更关心“到底什么是 FDE？”。

FDE 模式，起源于为美国情报部门搭建软件系统的需求。这个业务的挑战是，现实生活中没有任何人认识情报工作人员，即使认识，对方也不可能跟你聊具体工作内容。所以，Palantir 只能想象不同的场景，先做 demo，再收集反馈，重复多次。这个业务就没有办法和场景深度互动融合，做好定制。

这个过程让 Palantir 意识到：与其给每个场景单独做一个版本，或者在一个通用产品上打很多定制化的补丁，不如直接把产品做成高度可定制化的平台，再由前线部署工程师（FDE）带着产品进场，填补差距。Bob McGrew 打了一个比方：把路先铺成一条碎石路，总部的产品和工程团队负责做抽象、泛化，修成能服务接下来 5-10 个客户的高速公路。

听起来，这似乎和 SaaS 时代的项目制软件开发没有区别，这在互联网时代被认为是规模效应最差、应该尽量避免的商业模式。这也是 Palantir 被质疑最多的点：“这是一家永远无法规模化的咨询公司，而不是软件公司”。

（配图文字节选）
标题：AI SaaS “新巨头”案例：Palantir 与它的 FDE 模式
说明：Palantir 在 ChatGPT 发布前市值不到 150 亿美元，如今接近 5000 亿美元，位列美国上市公司第 18 名，超过了传统石油巨头和大多数银行。历史上没有公司以如此速度（从 150 亿到 5000 亿）比 Palantir 更快。11 月 4 日 Palantir 发布被称为“软件公司史上最佳业绩”的财报，当天股价大跌 8%。文章意在分析这家 AI SaaS 公司如何用 AI 改变业务逻辑并取得空前效果。

summary: MT argues that preparing data for AI involves many stakeholders and raises technical, security, governance, and legal questions most companies haven't resolved; many organizations adopt a "crawl, walk, run" approach to start small, limit exposure, and iterate.
key_points: Data readiness often means aggregating inputs from multiple parties (internal, partners, customers, even competitors), which creates governance and security concerns.
Companies lack clarity on approval and ownership structures (e.g., committee vs. CEO vs. legal vs. CTO/CIO).
Many organizations mitigate risk by starting small and scaling gradually ("crawl, walk, run") to monitor and limit exposure.
Questions remain about how to handle and secure AI outputs and who has final authority over data decisions.

raw_snippet: MT: I think the notion of getting data ready has a multitude of vectors to it. For example, most of us have been looking at data readiness as a consortium of input players that would provide data, so not just my own company, but then other partners maybe or even customer data or, like I said, competitive data at some point. If that's the case, then you've got governance concerns and questions. You've got security concerns if, in fact, I'm now going to share the output of my data or my core data with somebody else and contribute to maybe a market-based solution of some kind. MT：我认为“准备数据”这个概念有多重维度。例如，我们大多数人将数据准备视为由多个输入方组成的联合体来提供数据，因此不仅仅是我自己公司的数据，还有其他合作伙伴的数据，甚至客户数据，或者如我所说的，在某些时候可能还有竞争对手的数据。如果情况如此，那么就会出现治理方面的顾虑和问题。如果我现在要与他人共享我的数据输出或核心数据，并可能为某种基于市场的解决方案做出贡献，那就会产生安全方面的顾虑。

summary: 本文指出企业级 AI 落地受阻的一个核心原因是企业缺乏可被机器理解的“业务说明书”，Palantir 通过构建 Ontology 作为新的 Context Layer（包含结构性、操作性、行为性上下文）来为 AI 提供必要的语境，从而促进上层 AI 应用落地。Palantir 通过动词建模、RAG 知识库、流程挖掘及与 Databricks、Snowflake 等合作来完善该上下文层。
key_points: 企业没有系统化的、机器可读的业务描述，导致 AI 只能基于无语境的数据做统计性推断。
Semantic Layer 侧重数据的一致性和可读性，Context Layer 侧重让系统形成对企业运行方式的一致认知。
上下文层分为三类：结构性上下文（词汇表/对象关系）、操作性上下文（规章/流程）和行为性上下文（真实决策模式/流程挖掘）。
Palantir 的 Ontology 通过定义业务对象及其“能做/不能做/触发条件”的动词、构建 RAG 知识库，并借助流程挖掘与数据平台合作，形成完整上下文层以支持 AI 应用。
该赛道吸引了多类厂商（如 Snowflake、Databricks、SAP、Oracle、Celonis、Aris、Palantir、Atlan 等）进入，竞争将十分激烈。

raw_snippet: 之前 Palantir融合流程挖掘的背后：流程终于成为了不可替代的数据资产聊到Palantir通过流程挖掘丰富其Ontology数据。其最终的目的是构建一个全新的企业上下文层（Context Layer）。是企业级AI快速发展的这两年，语义层（semantic layer）和上下文层成为了众多厂商心目中解决企业级AI落地难点的解药。  Palantir 心目中的 Ontology表面上看起来像是传统数据治理的升级，但实际上，它试图解决的是一个更底层的问题：在 AI 参与决策之前，企业要把自己的业务世界结构化地表达清楚。  一、AI 落地受阻一大原因是企业没人说得清自己在干什么  大量研究MIT企业AI研究解读：农村包围城市表明企业 AI 项目普遍停留在演示和试点阶段，把视角从技术实现拉回到企业运行现实，厂商们发现了一个更核心的断层：企业自身并没有一个可被机器理解的业务说明书。  传统数据治理下的数据只能回答“发生了什么”，却无法解释“这意味着什么”。一个订单延迟的数据记录，对人来说可能立即联想到客户重要性、历史合作关系以及潜在的风险升级路径，但对 AI 而言，它只是一条数值变化的时间序列。  企业中真正影响决策是存在于流程执行中的隐性规则、跨部门协作的默契判断以及长期形成的经验偏好之中，而这些内容从未被系统性地建模和表达。当 AI 被直接接入数据层时，它面对的是一个缺乏语境的世界，只能通过统计和推断“猜测”下一步应该怎么做。  大家步入社会需要9年制义务教育；咨询公司或新人进入公司，需要足够的学习时间和成本。而AI作为还在牙牙学语的一员，也固然需要一个学习材料和融入过程。   二、Context Layer，AI时代的新解药  传统的数据治理解决的是技术问题：企业拥有大量分散在不同系统、不同数据库、不同业务域中的数据资产，于是通过数据中台或数据湖的方式，将这些数据集中到一个统一的平台中，并对表名、字段名、指标口径进行规范化标注，以避免“同名不同义”或“同义不同算”的情况反复出现。这个体系用现在的名称是语义层（Semantic Layer），其核心目标，是帮助分析师、业务人员和管理者正确使用数据。它强调的是可读性、可复用性以及跨系统的一致性，本质上仍然是围绕“数据”本身展开的治理。  上下文层（Context Layer）是AI时代的新产物。Semantic Layer 的目标是“让不同角色对同一数据形成一致理解”，那么上下文层的目标是“让系统对企业的运行方式形成一致认知”。  如果说我们学习一个新领域分三个阶段，专业词汇 > 理论知识 > 实践掌握，那上下文层也包含同样的三类信息。  1.结构性上下文（structural context），例如：词汇表。它定义了企业中的对象体系、核心概念及其关系结构，目标是基本语义一致性，为了让所有部门对同样的表单、指标有着同样的命名和理解提。很多企业从未做过结构性上下文的梳理。  2.操作性上下文（Operational context），例如：规章制度，流程文件。企业的用户手册，它定义了业务流程该如何运行，规则在什么条件下生效，哪些场景需要人工判断，为了让大家对企业运转有常识性的理解。大部分企业具有大量散落的操作性上下文，缺乏整体性的管理。  3.行为性上下文（Behavioral context），例如：真实数据。它刻画的是企业在长期运转过程中形成的真实决策模式，不同决策带

OpenAI 正在向其一些最大科技合作伙伴筹集巨额资金，以期筹集多达 1000 亿美元来满足其人工智能日益增长的需求。知情人士称，作为已有投资者且其芯片为 OpenAI 的 AI 模型提供算力的 Nvidia，正在洽谈投资最多 300 亿美元。  Microsoft, a longstanding backer with exclusive rights to sell OpenAI models to cloud customers, is in talks to invest less than $10 billion. And Amazon, which would be a new investor, is also in talks to invest significantly more than $10 billion, potentially even more than $20 billion. 长期支持者 Microsoft（对向云客户销售 OpenAI 模型享有独家权利）正在洽谈投资少于 100 亿美元。而作为潜在新投资者的 Amazon 也在洽谈投资，金额远超 100 亿美元，甚至可能超过 200 亿美元。

summary: Cowork gives Claude access to a user-selected folder so it can read, edit, and create files to perform tasks like reorganizing downloads, extracting expenses into a spreadsheet, or drafting reports from notes. It grants Claude more agency than a regular conversation—Claude makes a plan and carries it out while keeping the user informed—and is built on the same foundations as Claude Code to support many similar tasks in a more approachable, non-coding form.
key_points: Claude is granted access to a chosen folder and can read, edit, or create files there.
Example tasks: sort/rename downloads, compile expenses from screenshots into a spreadsheet, draft reports from scattered notes.
Operates with greater agency than a typical chat: it plans and steadily completes tasks while looping the user in.
Built on Claude Code foundations, enabling similar capabilities but aimed at non-coding workflows.
raw_snippet: How is using Cowork different from a regular conversation? In Cowork, you give Claude access to a folder of your choosing on your computer. Claude can then read, edit, or create files in that folder. It can, for example, re-organize your downloads by sorting and renaming each file, create a new spreadsheet with a list of expenses from a pile of screenshots, or produce a first draft of a report from your scattered notes.  In Cowork, Claude completes work like this with much more agency than you’d see in a regular conversation. Once you’ve set it a task, Claude will make a plan and steadily complete it, while looping you in on what it’s up to. If you’ve used Claude Code, this will feel familiar—Cowork is built on the very same foundations. This means Cowork can take on many of the same tasks that Claude Code can handle, but in a more approachable form for non-coding tasks.
